doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Playing after spinal surgery and Konitz's 'You can always simplify'
summary: After 1993 surgery left his right hand crippled he plays only rebuilt soprano sax; Konitz's advice to simplify shaped his playing, as on the 'Old Friends' duo record.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah, thank you for those answers. Has your melody conception changed over the years? You lost the use of your right arm and the fact that you managed to keep playing but in a different way, did it affect the way you think about melodies?

Yeah. Well I had my soprano, after I had my — I had surgery in 1993 that left my — to remove a spinal tumor that was life-threatening so that left my right hand basically crippled. I mean I have only a very limited use of my right hand so the only horn I could still play of the nine saxophones and flutes and clarinets I’ve played at one point, the only one I could still play was soprano saxophone. So I had a repairman, Perry Ritter, who is a great repairman, he rebuilt the horn with alternate keys so I could still play. But I guess as a result, you know I mean Lee Konitz one afternoon about eight or ten years ago Lee and I got together for lunch and we just went over to his apartment and just played improvised duets, just calling tunes for an hour or two. And he said something that I’ll never forget. He said, “You can always simplify.” And that’s one of the hippest bits of advice I’ve ever heard from an improvising musician. You can always simplify, and it’s true. I mean I only have a fraction of the facility on the horn that I used to, so as an improviser I’ve just learned to play simpler because I have to. For example, that record I did, the duo record I did with Marc Copland in 2008 called “Old Friends” I mean that’s just the two of us playing tunes that we like to play. And the track, I sent that to you, the tracks are long, man. I mean they’re anywhere from ten to fifteen minutes long for a duo. So I mean playing simpler doesn’t mean that you can’t play for a long period of time. You just learn to pace yourself in a different way. But I mean we just did that concert and you know just with as much spontaneity as possible. And after it was done I was

staggered at how long the tracks were. And I’d like to think that they’re not boring or not going on past their bedtime. But they’re really extended and it’s just the two of us. So I mean you learn to pace yourself in a different way.
